workflow.decision: When external behavior leaves implementation questions unresolved, look for legitimately accessible offline analysis artifacts. Record provenance and age before using them to refine hypotheses; representativeness of the deployed build remains a separate question.

When access appears blocked, identify the layer enforcing the restriction and the downstream consumer. Map their interpretation boundaries before treating an intermediary's denial as proof of consumer-side enforcement; semantic agreement remains an unresolved question.

Before inferring stronger impact, enumerate the environmental capabilities each hypothesis requires. If deployment policy denies a required connection, mark that hypothesis unsupported under that configuration and return to the underlying finding rather than promoting it to a stronger result.

Treat a published exception as scoped negative evidence: ask which guard caused rejection and whether that guard exists in the relevant dependency revision. Compare the narrow implementation slice across revisions; static guard presence or absence does not replace benign runtime validation of applicability.

tools.purpose: Compare a narrow implementation slice across dependency revisions to investigate whether a rejection guard is present.
tools.when: A published failure may depend on mitigation added after the installed revision; use comparable, authorized source artifacts before changing an applicability claim.

handoffs.when: An upstream access gate and downstream consumer interpret the same input independently, leaving enforcement equivalence unresolved.

limitations: The author used an older developer testing package, not an established equivalent of every deployed build. The article reports its later removal; public indexing is neither authorization nor artifact-integrity evidence.

Runtime/library compatibility and outbound-policy constraints are author reports tied to historical configurations. They were not measured here and cannot be generalized to current releases or other deployments.

Failure of a connection-dependent hypothesis does not establish repair of the underlying behavior or exhaustive non-exploitability. This extraction retains the constraint, not an alternate exploit route.
The source-revision comparison is narrow and does not establish all callers, package contents or runtime reachability. Static absence of a guard needs separate safe applicability evidence.

The article reports vendor fixes and uses static-file modification metadata as a coarse patch-status indicator. No shipped package or installed repair was verified here; advisory publication and header metadata are not deployment proof.

All vulnerability, execution and bounty outcomes remain source-author reports. This work only read the article and verified quotations; it did not obtain research packages, run exploit code or test any target.

candidate_additions.guidance: Separate implementation visibility from deployed applicability: authorized offline artifacts may reduce uncertainty, but record acquisition provenance, age and build-equivalence gaps before using their behavior to rank reachable surfaces.

For layered request handling, attach each policy check to the representation it actually sees and map the downstream consumer separately. Investigate semantic agreement with benign observations rather than assuming an intermediary's denial proves equivalent consumer enforcement.

Make environment capabilities explicit prerequisites of impact hypotheses. A denied required connection invalidates that hypothesis under the recorded policy, not the underlying finding; carry both the failed prerequisite and residual uncertainty forward.

Do not inherit a published exception as universal negative evidence. Identify its rejection guard, compare only the relevant implementation across comparable dependency revisions, and keep static applicability inference separate from benign runtime confirmation.
